doc_description: Johnson & Johnson’s 2022 Form 10-K (fiscal year ended January 1, 2023) filed with the SEC, reporting $94.9B in sales across Pharmaceutical, MedTech and Consumer Health, outlining the planned Consumer Health spin-off as Kenvue, the Abiomed acquisition, impending STELARA loss of exclusivity, extensive talc and opioid litigation and other key risks, along with audited financials, governance details, and share repurchase activity.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- Document type and scope: Johnson & Johnson’s Form 10-K annual report for the fiscal year ended January 1, 2023, filed with the U.S. SEC.
- Company and filing details: New Jersey corporation; Commission file number 1-3215; principal offices in New Brunswick, NJ; registrant phone number provided. Lists securities registered on the NYSE (common stock and several notes). Confirms status as a well-known seasoned issuer and large accelerated filer; complies with Exchange Act filing and interactive data requirements; auditor attestation of internal controls; not a shell company.
- Market and share data: Approximate public float of $472 billion as of the last business day of the most recent second fiscal quarter; 2,604,286,303 shares outstanding as of February 10, 2023.
- Incorporation by reference: Portions of the 2023 Proxy Statement incorporated into Parts I and III.
- Table of contents overview:
  - Part I: Business overview (segments, geography, raw materials, IP, trademarks, seasonality, competition, environment, regulation, human capital), Risk Factors, Properties, Legal Proceedings, Mine Safety, Executive Officers.
  - Part II: Market for common equity and related matters, MD&A, Market Risk disclosures, Financial Statements and Supplementary Data, Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants, Controls and Procedures, Other Information, Foreign jurisdiction inspection disclosures.
  - Part III: Directors, Executive Officers and Corporate Governance; Executive Compensation; Security Ownership; Certain Relationships and Related Transactions; Principal Accountant Fees and Services.
  - Part IV: Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedules; Form 10-K Summary; Signatures; Exhibit Index.
- Cautionary note on forward-looking statements: Explains the nature of forward-looking statements, associated assumptions, and that actual results may differ due to numerous risks; advises investors not to rely unduly and references Item 1A Risk Factors; states no obligation to update.
- Key risk categories summarized:
  - Product development, market success and competition: uncertainties in R&D, clinical outcomes, regulatory approvals, coverage/access, IP protection and challenges, patent expirations and loss of exclusivity, competitive dynamics, collaborations/licensing competition, and infringement allegations.
  - Product liability, litigation and regulatory activity: safety/efficacy concerns, withdrawals/recalls, reputational harm, litigation/government actions, adequacy of legal reserves, heightened industry scrutiny and penalties, compliance obligations, evolving laws and regulations (approval, IP, promotion, reimbursement/pricing, environment, sourcing), international compliance (e.g., EU MDR), tax law changes and audit scrutiny, and new accounting/SEC standards.
  - Strategic initiatives, market trends, and planned Consumer Health separation: pricing pressures from cost containment and payer consolidation, spending constraints, execution of growth strategy via external innovation and deals, realization of M&A/divestiture and restructuring benefits, timing and success of the Consumer Health separation, and the standalone prospects of the New Consumer Health Company.
  - Economic conditions, financial markets, and international operations: global operational risks, inflation, FX and interest rate volatility, trade policy changes and tariffs, international financial and political instability, pandemics (including COVID-19), climate change/extreme weather/natural disasters, and impacts of armed conflicts/terrorism.
  - Supply chain and operations: manufacturing and supply disruptions (internal and third-party), product shortages or market suspensions, IT/cybersecurity interruptions and breaches (including vendor systems), complexity and regulation of global supply chains, and risks to achieving supply chain restructuring benefits.

structure.summary:
- Overview: Johnson & Johnson is a New Jersey–incorporated holding company (since 1887) with about 152,700 employees and global operations focused on human health and well-being. Operating companies conduct business worldwide.

- Management structure: The Executive Committee oversees strategy, resource allocation, and the three segments—Consumer Health, Pharmaceutical, and MedTech (formerly Medical Devices). Day-to-day operations are decentralized, managed by local leadership in each subsidiary.

- Business segments: The company operates in Consumer Health, Pharmaceutical, and MedTech. Detailed segment financials are referenced to Item 7 (MD&A) and Note 17 (Segments and Geographic Areas).

- Consumer Health: Portfolio spans Skin Health/Beauty, Over-the-Counter (OTC) medicines, Baby Care, Oral Care, Women’s Health, and Wound Care. Notable brands include:
  - Skin Health/Beauty: Aveeno, Clean & Clear, Dr. Ci:Labo, Neutrogena, OGX
  - OTC: Tylenol, Sudafed, Benadryl, Zyrtec, Motrin IB, Nicorette (outside U.S.), Zarbee’s, Pepcid
  - Baby: Johnson’s, Aveeno Baby
  - Oral Care: Listerine
  - Women’s Health (outside North America): Stayfree, Carefree, o.b.
  - Wound Care: Band-Aid Brand, Neosporin
  Products are sold via eCommerce, retail outlets, and distributors globally.
  Strategic update: In November 2021, J&J announced plans to separate the Consumer Health business into a new publicly traded company (Kenvue) by the end of fiscal 2023.

- Pharmaceutical: Focus areas include Immunology, Infectious Diseases (HIV), Neuroscience, Oncology, Cardiovascular & Metabolism, and Pulmonary Hypertension. Medicines are prescription products distributed to retailers, wholesalers, distributors, hospitals, and healthcare professionals.
  Key products (with indications) include:
  - Remicade (infliximab) for immune-mediated inflammatory diseases
  - Simponi (golimumab) and Simponi Aria (golimumab IV) for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, ulcerative colitis; Simponi Aria also for pJIA (2+ years)
  - Stelara (ustekinumab) for plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis
  - Tremfya (guselkumab) for plaque psoriasis and active psoriatic arthritis
  - HIV therapies: Edurant (rilpivirine), Prezista (darunavir), Prezcobix/Rezolsta (darunavir/cobicistat), Symtuza (darunavir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide)
  - Concerta (methylphenidate HCl) for ADHD
  - Invega Sustenna/Xeplion and Invega Trinza/Trevicta (paliperidone palmitate) for schizophrenia (and schizoaffective disorder for Sustenna)
  - Risperdal Consta (risperidone LAI) for schizophrenia and maintenance of Bipolar I disorder
  - Zytiga (listing truncated in the excerpt)

- MedTech: Identified as a core segment (formerly Medical Devices); detailed product and market information not included in this partial excerpt.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: An investment in the Company’s common stock or debt securities involves risks and uncertainties.
structure.summary:
- Overview of extensive risk factors that could materially affect business, results, and financial condition across Johnson & Johnson’s segments.
- Competitive pressures across Pharmaceutical, MedTech, and Consumer Health, including loss of exclusivity, rapid innovation cycles, private-label competition, and high costs to acquire external assets.
- Manufacturing and supply chain vulnerabilities: quality or regulatory issues, labor shortages, disasters, raw material constraints, supplier disruptions; dependence on third‑party manufacturers and associated contractual, quality, IP, and capacity risks.
- Counterfeit and diverted products threatening patient safety, brand trust, revenues, and legal exposure.
- Impacts from global health crises (e.g., COVID-19): demand fluctuations, operational disruptions, supply chain stress, and uncertainties in vaccine development, approval, manufacturing scale-up, pricing, and access.
- Regulatory and legal risks: reimbursement and pricing pressures globally (including U.S. Inflation Reduction Act), extensive litigation exposure (e.g., talc, opioids), product safety issues leading to recalls and reputational harm, and heightened compliance scrutiny (cGMP, marketing, pricing, and fraud/abuse laws).
- Tax risks: potential adverse effects from global tax reforms (e.g., global minimum tax), changing statutory rates, and outcomes of audits/disputes.
- Intellectual property challenges: increasing patent validity and infringement disputes, IPR and biosimilar/ANDA challenges, and potential revenue loss from at‑risk launches.
- R&D and commercialization risks: high-cost, long-timeline development with uncertain outcomes; dependence on collaborations and acquisitions; market adoption, reimbursement, and post-approval safety/efficacy uncertainties.
- International operations risks: foreign exchange volatility, high inflation and devaluation (e.g., Argentina, Turkey, Venezuela), illegal importation of lower-priced drugs, and anti-bribery law exposure (FCPA, UK Bribery Act).
- Broader geopolitical and macro risks: trade barriers, regulatory variability, weaker IP protection in some jurisdictions, expropriation, social/political instability, terrorism, and pandemics.
- Credit rating risk: potential downgrades impacting liquidity, borrowing costs, and capital market access.
- Russia-Ukraine War impacts: sanctions/export controls, supply chain and demand disruption, FX volatility, IP enforcement limitations in Russia, and generally heightened risk environment.
- Planned separation of Consumer Health (Kenvue): execution timing and regulatory/tax-condition risks, significant transaction costs, uncertainty of expected benefits, stock price volatility, and potential tax liabilities if not tax-free.
- Talent and succession risks: competition for diverse, highly skilled employees and leadership continuity.
- Climate change risks: physical impacts on facilities and supply chain, water scarcity, evolving regulations increasing costs, and shifting customer preferences toward climate-friendly products.
- Cybersecurity and privacy risks: threats to IT systems and sensitive data across internal and third-party networks, potential operational/financial/regulatory impacts, increased cyber risk tied to geopolitical conflict, and expanding global data protection obligations (including cross‑border data flow restrictions).

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Results of Operations and Financial Condition
structure.heading: 7 Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Results of Operations and Financial Condition
structure.start_phrase:
Johnson & Johnson and its subsidiaries (the Company) have approximately 152,700 employees worldwide engaged in the research and development,
manufacture and sale of a broad range of products in the healthcare field.
structure.summary:
- Overview and structure: Johnson & Johnson operates globally across three segments—Consumer Health, Pharmaceutical, and MedTech—with ~152,700 employees. The Executive Committee manages strategy and resource allocation. The company competes intensely on innovation, IP protection, and consumer demand creation.

- Management objectives: Purpose-driven strategy anchored in “Our Credo”; focus on accessible, high-quality, innovative healthcare. New products from the past five years represented ~25% of 2022 sales. R&D investment was $14.6B in 2022. Emphasis on workforce diversity, agility, and enterprise-scale innovation.

- Consolidated 2022 sales: $94.9B, up 1.3% (volume +6.9%, price -0.8%, currency -4.8%). U.S. sales $48.6B (+3.0%); international $46.4B (-0.6%). Europe down 0.6% (operational +11.0%, currency -11.6%); Western Hemisphere ex-U.S. up 6.5%; Asia-Pacific/Africa down 2.8%. Three wholesalers represented ~16.5%, 13.0%, and 12.0% of total revenue.

- Consumer Health segment: Sales $15.0B (-0.5%; operational +3.6%, currency -4.1%). U.S. +1.3%; international -1.9% (operational +5.3%, currency -7.2%). OTC grew 7.2% (higher Cough/Cold/Flu, U.S. pricing, China consumption post-COVID restrictions); Skin Health/Beauty, Oral Care, Baby Care declined (supply constraints, competitive pressures, Russia suspension, China/EMEA headwinds). Women’s Health slightly down; Wound Care/Other down. Planned separation of Consumer Health (Kenvue) announced in 2021.

- Pharmaceutical segment: Sales $52.6B (+1.7%; operational +6.7%, currency -5.0%). U.S. +2.3%; international +1.0% (operational +11.9%, currency -10.9%). 
  - Immunology up (STELARA growth in IBD; TREMFYA strength), offset by REMICADE erosion from biosimilars. STELARA U.S. patent expires Sept 2023; loss of exclusivity expected to reduce sales.
  - Infectious Diseases down (lower PREZISTA family; COVID-19 vaccine growth ex-U.S. partially offset).
  - Neuroscience slightly down (INVEGA long-acting growth offset by RISPERDAL CONSTA decline and FX).
  - Oncology up strongly (DARZALEX and ERLEADA growth; declines in IMBRUVICA, ZYTIGA due to competition/LOE).
  - Pulmonary Hypertension roughly flat; OPSUMIT/UPTRAVI growth offset by declines in other products.
  - Cardiovascular/Metabolism/Other down (INVOKANA and PROCRIT/EPREX pressures).
  - 340B contract pharmacy policy update implemented; discount policy changes positively impacted 2022 sales.
  - Pipeline progress: multiple 2022 approvals/filings across CARVYKTI, ERLEADA, IMBRUVICA, teclistamab, talquetamab, CABENUVA (adolescents), STELARA (juvenile PsA), among others.

- MedTech segment: Sales $27.4B (+1.4%; operational +6.2%, currency -4.8%). U.S. +5.4%; international -2.3% (operational +6.9%, currency -9.2%).
  - Surgery down 1.2% (Advanced and General Surgery grew operationally on market recovery and new products, offset by FX).
  - Orthopaedics flat (operational +3.7% offset by FX; recovery in hips/knees, new tech, China volume-based procurement headwinds).
  - Vision up 3.4% (contact lenses and surgical growth from recovery, pricing, innovation).
  - Interventional Solutions up 8.3% (market recovery, innovation; includes late-December addition of Abiomed).

- Earnings and expenses: 2022 income before tax $21.7B (22.9% margin) vs. 2021 $22.8B (24.3%).
  - Cost of products sold rose as a percent of sales (COVID-19 vaccine manufacturing exit costs, FX in Pharma, commodity inflation), partially offset by Consumer Health supply chain benefits.
  - SG&A decreased as a percent of sales (lower brand marketing).
  - R&D expense $14.6B (15.4% of sales), slightly down; lower Pharma milestones.
  - IPR&D impairments: $0.8B for bermekimab (program terminated); prior year $0.9B for Ottava robotic platform delay (MedTech) with $1.5B remaining intangible under monitoring.
  - Other (income) expense net unfavorable by $1.4B vs. 2021, driven by Consumer Health separation costs, fair value losses on securities, COVID-19 vaccine exit, and lower divestiture gains; partially offset by lower litigation and employee benefit plan impacts.
  - Interest swung to net income ($214M) from expense on higher yields; average cash lower and debt higher due to Abiomed acquisition.

- Segment profitability:
  - Consumer Health margin improved to 19.6% (lower litigation—talc—, reduced marketing, supply chain benefits; offset by commodity inflation).
  - Pharmaceutical margin declined to 30.3% (COVID-19 vaccine exit costs, securities fair value loss, bermekimab IPR&D charge, lower divestiture gains, FX in COGS; partially offset by lower litigation, milestones, and marketing).
  - MedTech margin rose to 16.8% (lapping 2021 Ottava IPR&D charge), partially offset by higher pelvic mesh litigation and Abiomed acquisition costs.

- Restructuring: Global Supply Chain program completed in Q4 2022; cumulative ~$2.2B costs; achieved ~$0.8B annual pre-tax savings. 2022 pre-tax charges ~$0.5B.

- Taxes: Effective tax rate 17.4% (vs. 8.3%). ~$.5B net incremental international tax cost tied to Consumer Health separation in 2022; OECD Pillar Two adoption in EU (effective 2024/2025) under evaluation.

- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Cash & equivalents $14.1B (vs. $14.5B); marketable securities $9.4B (vs. $17.1B).
  - Operating cash flow $21.2B (driven by net earnings, non-cash items, working capital changes).
  - Investing cash use $12.4B (Abiomed acquisition ~$17.7B, CapEx $4.0B; net sales of investments $9.2B).
  - Financing cash use $8.9B (dividends $11.7B; buybacks $6.0B; net debt proceeds $7.5B).
  - Net debt $16.1B (vs. $2.1B); total debt $39.7B (due to Abiomed). TCJA R&D capitalization increased 2022 cash taxes by ~$1.2B.
  - $5B share repurchase program authorized Sept 2022; ~$2.5B repurchased by Jan 1, 2023.
  - Contractual obligations include TCJA amortization, debt maturities, and interest. Access to liquidity through two 364-day $10B revolving credit facilities; no material commitment fees.

- Market risk and hedging: Use of FX forwards and currency swaps to hedge exposures; sensitivity analyses show offsetting impacts between derivatives and underlying transactions. Interest rate risk modest on investment portfolio.

- Dividends: Increased for 60th consecutive year; $4.45 per share in 2022. Q1 2023 dividend declared $1.13 per share.

- Critical accounting policies: Revenue recognition (rebates, returns, promotions, collaborations), income taxes (deferreds, uncertain positions), legal/self-insurance contingencies, valuation of long-lived/intangible assets, employee benefits, stock-based compensation. Detailed accrual rollforwards for rebates/returns/promotions and reserves by segment provided.

- Economic/market factors: Responsible pricing; U.S. net price CAGR below CPI (2012–2022). Highly inflationary accounting for Argentina, Venezuela, and from Q2 2022, Turkey. Russia-Ukraine impact not material; suspension of personal care in Russia; continued supply of essential healthcare products. Ongoing FX, tax policy, healthcare cost containment, and IP/biosimilar challenges noted.

- Legal proceedings: Broad litigation portfolio managed; accruals recorded when losses are probable and estimable; outcomes not expected to materially affect financial position, but could impact results/cash flows in a period. Additional detail in Note 19.

- Common stock: Listed on NYSE (JNJ); 124,211 record holders as of Feb 10, 2023.

- Cross-references: Market risk disclosures tie to MD&A Financing and Market Risk and Note 1. Index to audited consolidated financial statements and reports included.

- Notional amounts outstanding:

  - All derivatives at fair value on balance sheet.
  - Changes recorded in earnings or OCI based on hedge designation.
  - Cash flow hedges use the forward method; amounts reclassified to earnings when hedged items affect results.
  - Fair value hedges: gains/losses on swaps and hedged debt recorded in interest expense.
  - Net investment hedges: gains/losses to CTA within AOCI; excluded components recognized in interest (income)/expense using the spot method.
  - Ongoing effectiveness assessment; discontinue hedge accounting if ineffective.

  - Net investment hedges (2022): Excluded component recognized in income $140m; amounts recognized in AOCI for cross-currency swaps; no reclassifications to income.

nodes.summary:
- The excerpt summarizes ongoing patent litigation involving Janssen products ZYTIGA and XARELTO.

- ZYTIGA (Canada):

- XARELTO (United States):
  - Starting March 2021, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and Bayer sued multiple generic companies in the District of Delaware for infringing U.S. Patent No. 10,828,310 (2.5 mg dose). Defendants include Dr. Reddy’s, Lupin, Taro, and Teva. Cases consolidated in October 2021; trial scheduled for May 2023.
  - Separate suits against Mylan in the Northern District of West Virginia (July 2021 and August 2022) were transferred by the MDL panel to Delaware; Mylan withdrew a motion to dismiss; no trial dates set.

  - Additional suit filed September 2022 in New Jersey against USV regarding ANDA for XARELTO 2.5, 10, 15, and 20 mg, asserting the ’310 and U.S. Patent No. 9,539,218 (’218); transferred to Delaware in November 2022. Plaintiffs seek injunctions tied to the respective patent expirations.

nodes.heading: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
nodes.start_phrase: We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheets of Johnson & Johnson and its subsidiaries (the “Company”) as of January 1, 2023 and January 2, 2022, and the related consolidated statements of earnings, of comprehensive income, of equity and of cash flows for each of the three fiscal years in the period ended January 1, 2023, including the related notes (collectively referred to as the “consolidated financial statements”).
nodes.summary:
- Independent auditor’s report by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP to Johnson & Johnson’s board and shareholders.
- Scope: Audits of consolidated financial statements (balance sheets as of Jan 1, 2023 and Jan 2, 2022; statements of earnings, comprehensive income, equity, and cash flows for the three fiscal years ended Jan 1, 2023) and audit of internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) as of Jan 1, 2023 under COSO 2013.
- Opinions: Unqualified (clean) opinions on the financial statements (fairly present in conformity with U.S. GAAP) and on ICFR (effective in all material respects).
- Basis for opinions: Management’s responsibility for the financial statements and ICFR; auditor independence and PCAOB registration; audits conducted under PCAOB standards to obtain reasonable assurance; description of audit procedures, risk assessment, testing, evaluation of estimates, principles, presentation, and ICFR design/operating effectiveness.
- Scope limitation/exclusion: Abiomed, Inc. (acquired in 2022) excluded from management’s ICFR assessment and the auditor’s ICFR audit; represents less than 1% of total assets and sales for FY2022.
- Definition and inherent limitations of ICFR: Purpose, components, and limitations including possible failure to prevent/detect misstatements and potential deterioration over time.
- Critical Audit Matters (CAMs):
  - U.S. pharmaceutical rebate reserves (Managed Care, Medicare, Medicaid): Significant variable consideration and judgment; $9.6 billion liability as of Jan 1, 2023; estimates based on contractual terms, historical experience, patient outcomes, trend analysis, and projected U.S. market conditions. Auditor procedures included testing controls, developing independent estimates using third-party pricing/market data and program terms, testing processed claims, and comparing independent estimates to management’s.
  - Litigation contingencies – Talc: Significant judgment on probability and estimability of losses; complexities and uncertainties across numerous legal factors; creation of LTL Management LLC to assume talc liabilities; Chapter 11 filing, stays/injunctions, transfers between courts, and the Third Circuit’s Jan 30, 2023 reversal directing dismissal of the LTL bankruptcy (with petition for rehearing). Auditor procedures included testing controls over loss assessments and disclosures, understanding processes, consultations with internal and external counsel, evaluating legal inquiry letters, assessing probability/estimability, and disclosure sufficiency.
- Report details: Signed by PwC, Florham Park, New Jersey; dated February 16, 2023; auditor of the company since at least 1920 (specific start year undetermined).

- The assessment as of January 1, 2023 was performed using the COSO 2013 Internal Control–Integrated Framework across control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring.
- The process involved extensive documentation, evaluation, and testing of the design and operating effectiveness of ICFR.
- The December 2022 acquisition of Abiomed, Inc. was excluded from the 2022 ICFR assessment scope per SEC guidance; its assets and sales each represented less than 1% of consolidated amounts.
- Management concluded ICFR was effective as of January 1, 2023.
- PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, an independent registered public accounting firm, audited the effectiveness of ICFR and issued its report.
- The report is signed by the CEO (Joaquin Duato) and CFO (Joseph J. Wolk).

nodes.start_phrase: Set forth below are line graphs comparing the cumulative total shareholder return on the Company’s Common Stock for periods of five years and ten years ending January 1, 2023, against the cumulative total return of the Standard & Poor’s 500 Stock Index, the Standard & Poor’s Pharmaceutical Index and the Standard & Poor’s Healthcare Equipment Index.

  - Ranking: S&P Pharma highest, then Healthcare Equipment, S&P 500, with J&J lowest.
  - Trend note: Despite a market pullback in 2022 for S&P 500 and Healthcare Equipment, J&J and Pharma posted gains versus 2021.

  - Ranking: Healthcare Equipment highest, then Pharma, J&J, and S&P 500.
  - Conclusion: Over 10 years, J&J slightly outperformed the broad market but trailed both healthcare sector indices.

- Overall takeaways: J&J underperformed all referenced indices over the recent 5-year period but delivered competitive long-term returns, modestly beating the S&P 500 over 10 years while lagging sector peers.

- Exhibit index for Johnson & Johnson’s Form 10-K detailing Regulation S‑K Item 601 exhibits, including key corporate, transactional, compensation, and disclosure documents.
- Corporate governance documents incorporated by reference: Restated Certificate of Incorporation and amendments; By-Laws.

- Executive compensation and benefit plan exhibits (many incorporated by reference): Long-Term Incentive Plans (2005, 2012, 2022) and related award agreements; executive incentive and deferred compensation plans; severance plan and amendments.
- XBRL exhibits: Inline XBRL instance and linkbases (Schema, Calculation, Label, Presentation, Definition) and cover page data (embedded).
- Auditor and officer exhibits: PwC consent; CEO and CFO certifications under Sections 302 and 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
- Availability statement: Shareholders may request copies of listed exhibits at no charge; certain exhibits/schedules omitted per Item 601.
- Full text of the Johnson & Johnson Excess Savings Plan (2022 Restatement):
  - Purpose: Unfunded, nonqualified deferred compensation plan for a select group of management/highly compensated employees to restore employer matching amounts limited by IRC Section 401(a)(17).
  - Eligibility: Automatic for employees eligible under the qualified Johnson & Johnson Savings Plan whose compensation exceeds the Section 401(a)(17) cap; loss of eligibility in the qualified plan disqualifies participation.
  - Benefits: Credited as the difference between the hypothetical maximum employer match absent the 401(a)(17) cap and the actual match under the cap; no employee contributions permitted.
  - Earnings and vesting: Deemed investment returns set by the Pension Committee; vesting mirrors the qualified plan; forfeiture of unvested amounts upon termination with limited reinstatement on rehire.
  - Payment triggers and form: Lump sum within 90 days after separation from service, death, or 409A-defined disability; special six‑month delay for specified employees under 409A; grandfathered pre‑12/15/2008 elections may apply after age 55.
  - Administration: Pension and Benefits Committee as Plan Administrator with discretionary authority, delegation rights, claims and appeals procedures, tax withholding, attorney‑client privilege protections, and non‑duplication of benefits across nonqualified plans.
  - Funding: Unfunded, general obligations of the company; no trust or segregation of assets.
  - Amendment/termination: Permitted without reducing accrued benefits or violating 409A; distributions on plan termination allowed to the extent compliant with 409A.
  - Miscellaneous: Anti‑assignment, 409A compliance intent, scrivener’s error correction authority, recovery of overpayments, New Jersey governing law, and no employment rights.
- Exhibit A to the plan: Transfer of liabilities for designated Consumer Health (Kenvue) employees to the Kenvue Excess Savings Plan in Q1 2023 (and subsequent transfers), preserving vesting, not treated as separation from service, and maintaining 409A compliance.
- Exhibit 21: Comprehensive list of U.S. and international subsidiaries as of January 1, 2023 (including ABIOMED and Kenvue entities), noting Johnson & Johnson is not a subsidiary of any other entity.
